passage: Note from Salma, operations coordinator. After Monday's review, where the manager criticised Kiran's slides in front of the whole team, Kiran spent lunch telling three colleagues that the manager was "clueless" and "enjoys humiliating people." I sat nearby. His voice was tight and his hands were shaking. I said nothing then. On Tuesday I asked if he wanted to hear how it looked from outside, and he said yes. I suggested he cool off, write down what he wanted to understand, and ask the manager for a private conversation. He went that afternoon. On Wednesday he told me the manager had explained what the client expected, which nobody had told him. He still felt stung that the review was in front of everyone, and he said so.

qa.q: What did Kiran call the manager at lunch?
qa.a: Kiran said the manager was "clueless" and "enjoys humiliating people."

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling after the review, and what shows it?
qa.a: Kiran felt humiliated and angry; his tight voice, shaking hands and venting to colleagues show it.

qa.q: Why was asking for a private conversation better than venting?
qa.a: It let Kiran hear what the client expected and clarify what was wanted, while venting spread resentment without solving anything.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen the review?
qa.a: Perhaps as ordinary feedback given without noticing how public it felt, and the later explanation of the client's expectations suggests the manager was willing to clarify.

grounding: An employee feels humiliated by criticism and vents to colleagues, then cools off and asks for a private conversation.

passage:
Tuesday night.

Today Binita stopped the stand-up and said, in front of all nine of us, "Saurabh, this dashboard is late again and the numbers don't match." Everyone looked at their shoes. My ears were burning. I said "noted" and nothing else.

At lunch I went to the pantry and let it all out to Farhan and Leela. She always does this, she enjoys it, she has favourites. They nodded and added their own stories. For ten minutes it felt good. Then it felt worse, like I'd poured petrol on something.

After work I walked the long way home, past the lake, and let myself calm down. Honestly, the numbers didn't match. What I hate is how it was said, and that I don't know what "on time" means to her.

So, plan: tomorrow morning I'll message Binita and ask for fifteen minutes alone to understand what she needs and by when. No pantry speeches first.

qa.q: Who did Saurabh vent to in the pantry?
qa.a: Saurabh vented to Farhan and Leela.

qa.q: How can you tell Saurabh felt humiliated at the stand-up?
qa.a: Saurabh's ears were burning, everyone looked at their shoes, and Saurabh could only say "noted"; the diary shows shame and anger at being criticised in front of nine people.

qa.q: What small step is Saurabh planning, and why is it wiser than more venting?
qa.a: Saurabh plans to ask Binita for a private fifteen-minute talk to clarify expectations; this addresses the real problem instead of feeding resentment with colleagues.

qa.q: What would change if Binita heard about the pantry venting before the private talk?
qa.a: Binita might feel undermined and become defensive, making it much harder to have a calm conversation about expectations.

grounding: Shows a young employee who feels humiliated by a boss's public criticism, vents, then cools off and plans a private conversation to clarify expectations.
